question: Can an offline-trained DeepONet replace a locally expensive fine-scale solver inside an iterative FEM domain-decomposition loop, and do the paper's equations, experiments, artifacts, and current literature establish accurate, convergent, generalizable, and amortized-fast multiscale mechanics simulation?

key_findings.claim: The paper presents a concrete and reusable hybrid-solver interface rather than a monolithic learned simulator.
key_findings.evidence: A branch network encodes sampled interface data, a trunk network evaluates space or time coordinates, and their dot product supplies a subdomain field or derivative. FEM and DeepONet then exchange Dirichlet, Neumann, or Robin information in an iterative Schwarz-like loop. This separation between solver, learned operator, and interface protocol is the work's clearest contribution.

key_findings.claim: Only the hyperelastic benchmark couples FEM to a surrogate learned from a different particle-based model.
key_findings.evidence: Table 1 identifies FEM as the DeepONet training source for Poisson, heat, and elastoplasticity; the hyperelastic case alone trains on SPH. The first two are same-equation FEM replacement tests, and elastoplasticity replaces a nonlinear FEM region with operators while retaining linear FEM outside. Broad heterogeneous-multiscale language should therefore be read as a proposed framework illustrated by one FEM-SPH example, not four independent cross-scale demonstrations.

key_findings.claim: The paper demonstrates several interface-condition configurations, but it does not validate arbitrary coupling schemes or geometries.
key_findings.evidence: The four examples cover overlapping D-D and R-D plus non-overlapping N-D and R-D/R-N variants, all on fixed simple geometries. No moving interface, topology change, geometry distribution, multiple learned patches, noisy measurement interface, or coupled stochastic dynamics is tested. The discussion itself lists geometry variation, fracture motion, noisy particle data, and length/time-scale separation as future work.

key_findings.claim: The general relaxation update reverses the model weights between the prose and Algorithm 1.
key_findings.evidence: Page 6 defines the relaxed condition as (1-theta) times model I plus theta times model II. Algorithm 1 on page 7 instead uses (1-theta) times model II plus theta times model I. The Poisson specialization on page 9 follows the prose ordering. At theta=0.5 the formulas coincide, but the theta=0.25 and 0.75 comparisons in Figure 6 depend on which definition was implemented; no code resolves the ambiguity.

key_findings.claim: The prose definition of the general Robin information freezes traction at its initial value and mixes iteration indices.
key_findings.evidence: Page 6 defines h for models I and II using u at iteration n but T at iteration 0, even while labeling the quantity n+1. Algorithm 1 instead forms model-II h from both u and T at n+1. A method implemented literally from the prose would never update its Neumann contribution, so the formal algorithm is not reproducible without choosing an interpretation.

key_findings.claim: Algorithm 1 misdefines its interface boundaries and initializes the learned model at the wrong interface coordinate.
key_findings.evidence: The pseudocode sets Gamma 1 equal to the full boundary of model I and Gamma 2 to the full boundary of model II, whereas the overlapping Poisson domain has an outer boundary Gamma 0 in addition to its internal Gamma 1. Its initialization also sets model II at x1 even though model II receives the model-I condition at x2/Gamma 2. Figure 4 and Equations 8-9 use the narrower, sensible interface definitions, contradicting the supposedly general pseudocode.

key_findings.claim: The Poisson learned-subdomain statement cites an outer boundary equation that does not bound that subdomain.
key_findings.evidence: Page 9 says the neural subdomain Omega-NN is governed by Equations 6 and 7 together with Equation 9. Equation 7 is the outer Gamma-0 condition of the global or FEM-side problem and is not a boundary of Omega-NN in Figure 4. Under the displayed decomposition, the local neural statement should use its governing equation and the interface condition in Equation 9, not the unrelated outer boundary.

key_findings.claim: The stated convergence criterion is not the criterion used to substantiate most convergence plots.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 3 stops on the sum of successive full-subdomain iterate differences and leaves epsilon unspecified. Figures 6, 10, and 13 instead plot errors against an unavailable ground-truth solution and describe truth-relative thresholds as stopping criteria. A deployed solver cannot use those truth errors, and the paper neither reports actual Equation-3 stopping traces nor proves that the two criteria are equivalent.

key_findings.claim: The paper offers empirical examples, not a guarantee of convergence for neural-operator coupling.
key_findings.evidence: No theorem bounds surrogate error, interface contraction, or stability under distribution shift. The discussion uses 'guaranteed convergence' language while also stating that a poorly trained operator, poor normalization, or an unsuitable Robin coefficient can cause slow convergence or divergence. Figure 13 explicitly shows R=5 failing to converge.

anchors.section: Discussion on guaranteed convergence and pitfalls

key_findings.claim: The Poisson benchmark supports narrow in-distribution feasibility, not the claim that coupling error is negligible in general.
key_findings.evidence: For one displayed unseen alpha=5 boundary function, the interface relative error is about 0.07 percent and the field plots visually agree. The paper provides no repeated field-level error table, no uncertainty, no solver-tolerance sweep, and no direct comparison against a conventional FE-FE Schwarz implementation at matched discretization. The successful case shows the loop can work, but not its reliability distribution.

key_findings.claim: The phrase 'maximum absolute error less than 1%' is dimensionally malformed.
key_findings.evidence: Page 9 describes the third-column absolute-difference field as a percentage even though no normalization is defined for that field. The text later reports a separate relative interface error, so the absolute and relative metrics are being conflated rather than specified consistently.

key_findings.claim: The claim that FEM interpolation dominates Poisson error is not isolated experimentally.
key_findings.evidence: The paper attributes larger outer-domain errors and the post-300-example plateau to boundary interpolation, but it supplies no exact-interface baseline, interpolation-order sweep, mesh refinement, operator-oracle substitution, or error decomposition. The explanation is plausible, yet remains an inference from a plateau rather than a controlled ablation.

key_findings.claim: The Robin derivative regularizer is not defined as a complete scalar training objective.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 11 prints a squared pointwise difference between predicted and true normal derivatives with x on Gamma 1, but gives no sum, integral, average, sampling rule, normalization, or weight relative to the MSE in Equation 2. Consequently the loss magnitude and training contract cannot be reconstructed from the paper.

key_findings.claim: The Poisson out-of-distribution result is asymmetric and exposes a substantial high-frequency failure mode.
key_findings.evidence: The model is trained at alpha=5. Rougher functions with alpha below 5 produce errors rising toward roughly 10 percent, while alpha above 5 is smoother and remains below about 1 percent. Calling the complete alpha=1 to 10 sweep generalization obscures that one direction is an easier smoothness shift and the harder direction degrades by about an order of magnitude.

key_findings.claim: The heat section repeatedly calls a relaxed solution value a flux.
key_findings.evidence: The FEM-to-DeepONet information is K times the spatial derivative, but Equation 16 relaxes u values from FEM and NN. The surrounding prose names the resulting tilde-u quantity an 'interfacial flux' and says convergence of the flux controls the loop. This value/derivative confusion makes the N-D transmission contract ambiguous.

key_findings.claim: The heat interface is labeled N-D although the paper's declared ordering makes it D-N.
key_findings.evidence: The methodology defines the first letter as Model I/FEM and the second as Model II/DeepONet. Table 1 and the heat section call the coupling N-D, but Equation 15 gives FEM a Dirichlet trace while DeepONet receives the FEM flux as a Neumann input. Under the paper's own convention the implemented routing is D-N, so the taxonomy and executable boundary contract disagree.

key_findings.claim: The printed heat update is not an unambiguous backward-Euler inner iteration.
key_findings.evidence: FEM advances from the converged prior-time state u-infinity,k, but the neural update uses u at indices n,k as its base while its learned diffusion term is indexed n+1,k+1. If u-n,k changes during the inner coupling loop, the formula repeatedly advances the time state; if it is intended to stay frozen, that invariant is never stated. The same section calls the scheme backward Euler and later calls its implementation explicit, without executable pseudocode or a consistency/stability analysis.

key_findings.claim: The heat operator target can differ by a factor of ten under the paper's own notation.
key_findings.evidence: The heat section alternates between K times u-x and bare u-x as the interface input, and between K times u-xx and bare u-xx as the learned output; Figures 7c and C.17 omit K while the prose includes it, with K fixed at 0.1. It also invokes an undefined heat interface Gamma 1 after defining only Gamma and Gamma 0. These are material type-and-scale contradictions, not cosmetic notation, because two literal implementations train targets separated by a factor of ten.

key_findings.claim: The heat extrapolation experiment is too narrow to establish long-horizon dynamic generalization.
key_findings.evidence: Training derivatives cover t=0 to 1 with dt=0.1 and the plot extends to t=10 for one diffusion coefficient and one family of smooth initial conditions. Diffusive solutions rapidly decay toward a nearly stationary state, so late absolute error can remain small without preserving rich dynamics. No parameter shift, step-size shift, high-frequency initial condition, conservation diagnostic, rollout baseline, or repeated-case uncertainty is reported.

key_findings.claim: The elastoplastic training boundary condition is described inconsistently as displacement and traction.
key_findings.evidence: Page 16 says 1,000 displacement boundary conditions are sampled on the top edge. Figure 9 calls the applied quantity a traction t0, and Appendix D.2 explicitly defines a random non-uniform tension t0(x). The training input at the internal interface is displacement, but that does not repair the contradiction over how the global simulations were excited.

key_findings.claim: Independent stress-component DeepONets do not enforce the governing mechanics used to derive traction.
key_findings.evidence: Three separate networks predict sigma11, sigma12, and sigma22 from interface displacement. Their outputs are not constrained to satisfy equilibrium, compatibility, constitutive response, yield consistency, symmetry beyond selecting three components, or a common energy potential. Traction assembled from individually accurate components can therefore be nonphysical or amplify interface error, yet no residual or admissibility audit is reported.

key_findings.claim: The elastoplastic output contract switches from stress to strain without defining the missing quantities.
key_findings.evidence: The main text says three independent networks output Cauchy stresses sigma11, sigma12, and sigma22. Figure C.17 instead labels the corresponding elastoplastic outputs epsilon11, epsilon12, and epsilon22, while Figure 10 reports neural equivalent plastic strain without specifying a plastic-strain network or a derivation from the stated outputs. The reported MSE values therefore cannot be assigned unambiguously to stress, total strain, or plastic-state targets.

key_findings.claim: The elastoplastic evidence consists of point estimates from a fixed geometry with no disclosed holdout protocol.
key_findings.evidence: The paper reports 1,000 generated simulations but does not state the train/test split for this example, random seeds, repeated training runs, or a distribution of coupled-case errors. One typical field comparison has sub-10-percent maxima away from singular regions and sub-2-percent interface errors, while the convergence curve reaches a plateau after four iterations. These are useful feasibility numbers but not a reliability estimate.

key_findings.claim: The hyperelastic section contains an elastoplastic copy error in its output description.
key_findings.evidence: After saying DeepONets predict first Piola-Kirchhoff stress for the HGO hyperelastic material, page 21 says the predictions are used to calculate equivalent plastic strain and von Mises stress. Equivalent plastic strain belongs to the preceding elastoplastic model and has no defined role in the hyperelastic formulation. This weakens confidence that the implementation contract was transcribed carefully.

key_findings.claim: Figure 12's caption misidentifies its neural prediction as a second FEM result.
key_findings.evidence: The page-21 body says Figure 12 compares FEM and neural-network solutions, and the middle P22 panel is visibly labeled NN. The page-22 caption nevertheless calls column two a prediction from FEM for both displacement and P22. This is another output-provenance error in the principal heterogeneous benchmark's visual contract.

key_findings.claim: The two hyperelastic interface operators are not required to be reciprocal or energy-consistent.
key_findings.evidence: Net-u2s maps interface displacement to stress, while Net-s2u maps traction to displacement, and their outputs are combined in the Robin method. They are trained separately with pointwise MSE and no cycle-consistency, virtual-work, monotonicity, material-symmetry, equilibrium, or common-potential constraint. The two learned maps can disagree even when each has small average test error.

key_findings.claim: The hyperelastic Robin prose reverses both learned maps after defining them.
key_findings.evidence: Page 21 defines Net-u2s as displacement to first-Piola stress or traction and Net-s2u as traction to displacement. Page 23 then says traction and displacement are sent to Net-u2s and Net-s2u, respectively, and describes the outputs as displacement and traction. That reverses both maps, leaving a literal Robin implementation incompatible with the network definitions.

key_findings.claim: The stated two-fiber HGO configuration duplicates one direction rather than demonstrating diverse reinforcement directions.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 30 sums two fiber groups, but both alpha1 and alpha2 are set to pi/2 with zero dispersion. The two fourth invariants are therefore identical under the written definition. This can represent doubled weight in one vertical direction, but it does not exercise distinct anisotropic fiber families despite the phrase 'diverse directions.'

key_findings.claim: Treating SPH as ground truth is not justified by a discretization or solver-convergence study.
key_findings.evidence: The paper declares the full SPH solution ground truth, yet Appendix B offers only one qualitative FEM-SPH overlay, with visible traction discrepancies attributed to numerical integration and no norm, refinement, energy, or momentum check. Its caption says the same Dirichlet condition is imposed on the top and circle although the panel and prose use top traction plus interface displacement, and the prose calls SPH dashed although the plot uses point markers. Agreement with one unverified SPH discretization supports coarse code-to-code consistency, not continuum truth.

key_findings.claim: The arXiv-v1 headline timing is an online inference comparison, not an end-to-end or amortized speedup study.
key_findings.evidence: Table 3 of the pinned arXiv v1 compares roughly four hours for one time-dependent SPH call on a static problem against less than one second for its trained surrogate. It omits 900 training and 100 held-out SPH simulations, one million optimization steps, preprocessing, total interface iterations, and a break-even calculation; it also does not disclose whether common FEM work, transfer, synchronization, setup, and I/O are included equivalently. At the displayed rate, training-data generation alone is roughly 3,600 serial hours and all 1,000 experimental cases roughly 4,000 hours, implying about 900-1,000 replaced SPH calls before neural training costs under the simplest serial assumption. Actual parallelism is unreported.

key_findings.claim: The later journal author manuscript adds an amortization analysis absent from the pinned arXiv v1.
key_findings.evidence: The later journal author manuscript adds Appendix C formulas for training-time ratio, execution-time ratio, and break-even predictions. Its elastoplastic example uses Cs=30 seconds, Ns=1,000, Ct=3,720 seconds, and Ce=0.0014 seconds to report Rt=0.124, Re=4.6e-5, and Ne*=1,124 predictions. The printed Ne*=Ns+Ct/Cs neglects inference cost; exact cost equality gives (Ns Cs+Ct)/(Cs-Ce)=1,124.052, a negligible difference here because Ce/Cs is about 4.67e-5 but still an approximation. The manuscript also cautions that lower neural heat MSE from t=2 to 7 reflects oscillatory FEM error and does not prove better generalization. These additions repair two arXiv-v1 omissions but do not provide a matched hyperelastic end-to-end protocol.

key_findings.claim: The timing comparison lacks enough protocol detail to reproduce even its online number.
key_findings.evidence: ArXiv v1 gives no CPU/GPU model, SPH particle count, FEM mesh size, precision, software version, solver tolerances, number of time steps, warmup, repeats, synchronization, inclusion boundary, or variance. In particular, it does not say whether common FEM work, transfer, setup, and I/O are timed equivalently. It also acknowledges that the SPH baseline is a time-dependent solver used for a static task and supplies no static SPH, fine-FEM, reduced-order, homogenization, or FE-FE domain-decomposition runtime baseline.

key_findings.claim: The SPH kernel definition in Equation A.2 has overlapping branches and omits the outside-support case.
key_findings.evidence: The cubic branch is written for Rj<h and the zero branch for Rj<=h. Those conditions overlap below h, while no branch covers Rj>h. The same displayed three-dimensional Spiky kernel uses normalization 10/(pi h^6), whereas the cited Rausch implementation gives 15/(pi h^6); 10 belongs to a two-dimensional form with h^5. The printed support and dimensional normalization therefore cannot both be implemented as claimed.

key_findings.claim: The SPH kernel-gradient formula loses its spatial direction under the notation defined in the paper.
key_findings.evidence: Rj is introduced as the scalar distance between particles, but Equation A.5 multiplies the radial derivative by Rj/Rj, which is one rather than a direction vector. A gradient requires a separation vector divided by its magnitude. The types in Equations A.4-A.7 therefore do not close as printed.

key_findings.claim: The printed SPH internal-force equation uses the same i-dependent kernel gradient for both particle terms.
key_findings.evidence: Equation A.14 subtracts Pi and Pj contributions while writing both corrected gradients at undefined Ri. The cited Ganzenmueller formulation instead uses distinct i-centered and j-centered correction-gradient terms evaluated on opposite separation vectors, so the displayed target equation omits the distinct j contribution. Equation A.11 also introduces undefined lowercase rj; Equation A.15 introduces undefined delta-i and delta-j and again writes scalar rj/rj where a direction is required. Together with an A-inverse versus Ai notation change, the appendix is not an executable specification of the claimed generator.

key_findings.claim: The SPH training-data generator omits parameters that its cited implementation treats as material to stability.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix A does not report hourglass coefficient or stiffness, density, particle spacing, smoothing length, time step, damping or viscosity, or a dynamic stopping rule. Its constitutive notation also switches from the main text's mu and K to c and K0 while saying parameters are the same, without a mapping. The cited Rausch implementation specifies, among other choices, hourglass alpha=50, hourglass stiffness equal to the initial material modulus, and smoothing lengths near three to four particle spacings, so these omissions block reconstruction rather than merely polishing it.

key_findings.claim: Several additional SPH appendix equations change tensor types or use undefined symbols.
key_findings.evidence: Equation A.9 tensor-products a scalar Rj and switches from the previously defined inverse correction to Ai without an indexed inverse. Equation A.11 writes tensor Fi like the componentwise derivative of xi with respect to Xi and uses undefined lowercase rj. Equation A.15 introduces undefined delta-i and delta-j and again reduces a direction to rj/rj. Equation A.17 introduces Ei locally without definition and changes material parameters from mu and K to c and K0 without a mapping. These independent defects persist beyond the three headline kernel and force errors.

key_findings.claim: The random-field generator is underdefined and singular at its zero Fourier mode.
key_findings.evidence: Equation D.1 sets gamma to the norm of k raised to negative alpha, which diverges at k=0. The main text calls alpha a correlation length, while Appendix D calls gamma a correlation function; the cited Lang-Potthoff construction instead uses a spectral density, making alpha here a spectral-decay or smoothness exponent. The heat section separately states correlation length 0.3, while Appendix D says heat uses alpha=5 without any length-scale parameter. Together with omitted zero-mode handling, domain, grid, normalization, real symmetry, and seeds, the input distributions are not reconstructible. The source TeX's commented TODO confirms the missing compact/periodic and OOD contract.

key_findings.claim: The paper does not release the computational artifacts required to reproduce its results.
key_findings.evidence: The official arXiv source archive contains TeX, bibliography files, and 23 static raster figures, but no solver or training code, raw data, weights, configurations, logs, or figure-generation scripts. Exact-title, identifier, publisher, and arXiv routes expose no official paper repository or supplement as of 2026-08-24. The first author's unlinked sph_solid_mech repository is plausible scratch lineage but has no root README, license, environment, tests, CI, DeepONet, four-benchmark pipeline, checkpoints, or configurations; its tutorial README is only a heading. Its HGO example has different geometry and runtime, none of the paper's 23 images match, and scripts contain missing files, obsolete APIs, and inconsistent names. It is not a reproducible paper artifact.

key_findings.claim: Even the adjacent public SPH scratch case depends on an unreleased custom solver and internally drifting configurations.
key_findings.evidence: The candidate repository's successful HGO inputs invoke custom STRENGTH-HGO and EOS-HGO commands absent from the contemporaneous stock LAMMPS revision. Historical repository commits point lmp-serial symlinks to a private user path and later delete them, while the author's public LAMMPS fork remains upstream. One committed input sets hourglass 50 while its paired log records zero; other cases mix SI units with GPa/mm/ms comments, apply abrupt dynamic loading, divide reaction force by a geometry-inconsistent 20, and provide no equilibrium, energy, or refinement rule. Thus even this adjacent constitutive path cannot be replayed end to end, much less the paper's neural coupling.

key_findings.claim: ArXiv v1 reports architecture and step counts but omits essential training controls.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix C of the pinned arXiv v1 states four-layer fully connected subnetworks, tanh activations, widths of 100 or 150, interface inputs of 51-120 points, 100,000 steps for Poisson and heat, and one million for elastoplasticity and hyperelasticity. It omits optimizer, learning-rate schedule, batch construction, initialization, normalization transform, most splits, early stopping, seeds, hardware, framework version, and model selection. The later author manuscript adds that neural networks used an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2060 and FEM data generation used two six-core Intel Core i7-8700 CPUs, but still does not supply the missing training contract or SPH timing hardware.

key_findings.claim: Training and test MSE point estimates do not establish statistical reliability of the coupled solver.
key_findings.evidence: Figures C.16-C.17 provide point learning curves and MSE values but no uncertainty across initialization, resampled data, meshes, or coupled cases. Figure C.16 shows only one train/test curve per mechanics problem although elastoplasticity has three component networks and hyperelasticity has six, without saying whether a curve is selected or aggregated. Figure C.17 prints hyperelastic P21 test MSE as '1,798 times 10^-8' while neighboring decimals use points, leaving a likely 1.798 locale or typography ambiguity. Low componentwise MSE does not bound interface contraction, force balance, long-horizon drift, or worst-case error.

key_findings.claim: The paper's generalization evidence varies boundary functions within fixed problem families rather than testing new mechanics regimes.
key_findings.evidence: Geometry, material law, decomposition, solver, discretization, and physical parameters remain fixed within each benchmark. The main shifts are new draws from the same family, an alpha sweep for Poisson, and time beyond the derivative-data window for one heat equation. There is no transfer across geometry, material, loading scale, mesh, particle resolution, PDE coefficient, or subdomain placement.

key_findings.claim: The paper-time first-attempt claim is narrower than the broad novelty rhetoric, and later work substantially strengthens the missing guarantees.
key_findings.evidence: The direct combination of a neural operator subdomain with a conventional numerical subdomain in a concurrent interface iteration appears plausibly novel in the authors' 2022 framing. However, operator-based multiscale surrogates, DeepM&Mnet compositions, learned constitutive homogenization, learned and classical domain decomposition, and particle-continuum coupling were established ingredients. Later FE-neural-operator, NOEM, learning-based domain-decomposition, reliability, error-estimation, OOD, and UQ papers directly address geometry, consistency, residual convergence, amortization, and uncertainty gaps left open here.

key_findings.claim: The most durable systems insight is to treat a learned subdomain as a boundary-condition service with explicit numerical contracts.
key_findings.evidence: The discussion observes that a network can predict only interface information when interior details are unnecessary. Recasting that insight as a typed service makes solver inputs, outputs, residuals, admissibility, uncertainty, and fallback criteria testable independently of network architecture. The paper sketches this modular view but does not implement its contracts or certification gates.

method.core_idea: Train a neural operator offline to emulate the expensive local model, then deploy it as one subdomain solver inside a conventional iterative domain-decomposition method while retaining FEM for the coarse or homogeneous region.
method.mechanism: DeepONet encodes discretized interface functions with a branch network and evaluation coordinates with a trunk network. For each online iteration, FEM solves its subdomain under the current interface condition, transmits displacement, derivative, or traction to the learned subdomain, DeepONet predicts a field or complementary interface quantity, and a fixed or Aitken-relaxed update supplies the next FEM boundary condition. Four fixed-geometry examples instantiate overlapping D-D/R-D and non-overlapping N-D/R-D/R-N variants.
assumptions: The expensive fine-scale response is localized in a subdomain known before simulation.
Training interface functions cover the online boundary and initial conditions sufficiently well.
Componentwise operator error remains small under repeated coupling and time marching.
The learned interface map preserves equilibrium, compatibility, constitutive admissibility, and material symmetries even when these are not encoded in the loss.
A suitable relaxation parameter or Robin coefficient makes the coupled map contractive.
Interpolation between FEM boundaries and DeepONet sensors does not dominate or destabilize the iteration.
The truth-independent successive-iterate stopping rule tracks actual solution error.
Separate displacement-to-stress and traction-to-displacement operators are mutually consistent.
SPH data are sufficiently converged to serve as reference truth.
The cost of generating fine-scale data and training can be amortized across enough online queries.
Fixed geometry, material, discretization, and subdomain results transfer to the intended deployment regime.
Normalization statistics remain valid under online distribution shift.
The printed relaxation, heat-stepping, random-field, and SPH equations can be repaired to match the unavailable implementation.
Stress, strain, and plastic-state labels in the elastoplastic figures can be reconciled with the three stated stress operators.
Pointwise train/test MSE is an adequate proxy for stable coupled-solver behavior.
A time-dependent SPH baseline for a static problem represents the relevant conventional cost.
Noisy or stochastic microscopic dynamics can be learned despite being deferred rather than tested.

techniques.role: Approximate maps from sampled interface functions to fields, stresses, displacements, or spatial derivatives.
Alternate numerical and learned subdomain solves while exchanging interface conditions.
Blend interface information with fixed theta or Aitken updates.
Combine value and derivative or traction information to accelerate selected coupling cases.
Retain a conventional variational solver in the coarse or homogeneous region and generate three training sources.
Generate the sole heterogeneous fine-model dataset for the hyperelastic example.
Sample Poisson, heat, and hyperelastic excitations from Gaussian random fields.
Learn the heat diffusion term rather than the full spatiotemporal solution operator.
Use separate operators for elastoplastic or hyperelastic stress components.
Expose a learned subdomain as an artificial boundary-condition provider.
Cross-check all pages, visuals, equations, source TeX, artifact availability, and current primary literature.

evaluations.setting: Overlapping 2D Poisson decomposition with an alpha=5 unseen boundary function and theta=0.5
evaluations.metric: Field differences and interface relative error
evaluations.result: The displayed typical case visually agrees with the full-domain FEM solution and reports roughly 0.07 percent relative interface error, but no repeated field-level uncertainty or matched FE-FE baseline is supplied.

evaluations.setting: Poisson interface strategy and relaxation sweep
evaluations.metric: Iterations to a stated truth-relative error threshold
evaluations.result: Fixed Dirichlet theta values 0.25, 0.5, and 0.75 reportedly require 37, 18, and 12 iterations; Aitken is slightly faster than theta=0.75 and Robin-Aitken reaches small error in two iterations. The relaxation-order contradiction and use of ground truth leave the operational comparison underdetermined.
evaluations.baseline: Fixed-theta D-D, Dirichlet-Aitken, and Robin-Aitken variants.

evaluations.setting: Poisson random-field smoothness shift from alpha=1 to 10 after training at alpha=5
evaluations.metric: Minimum relative interface error over 50 cases per alpha
evaluations.result: Errors fall from around 10 percent for rough alpha=1 inputs to below 1 percent at alpha=5 and remain stable for smoother inputs, showing asymmetric rather than robust two-sided OOD behavior.

evaluations.metric: Box plots of interface relative error over 50 cases
evaluations.result: Median error improves from 100 to roughly 300 examples and then plateaus; the paper attributes the plateau to interpolation without an isolating ablation.
evaluations.baseline: DeepONets trained with different numbers of fine-solver cases.

evaluations.setting: 1D heat equation, derivative data from t=0 to 1 and coupled rollout to t=10
evaluations.metric: Pointwise solution trace and FEM/DeepONet MSE over time
evaluations.result: The single displayed rollout remains visually close while MSE grows slowly, but the value/flux and inner-loop time-index ambiguities prevent exact reproduction and the late-time diffusive state is an easy extrapolation regime.
evaluations.baseline: Full-domain FEM solution for one coefficient and initial-condition family.

evaluations.setting: Fixed-geometry elastoplastic plate with a nonlinear inner region
evaluations.metric: Stress, equivalent plastic strain, interface displacement/traction error, and iteration history
evaluations.result: A typical case reports maximum errors below 10 percent away from singular regions, interface errors below 2 percent, and a plateau after four iterations. No train/test split, seed, repeated-case distribution, or mechanics-residual metric is given.

evaluations.setting: Fixed-geometry hyperelastic FEM-DeepONet coupling with the operator trained on 900 of 1,000 SPH cases
evaluations.metric: Displacement, P22, and interface displacement/traction comparison
evaluations.result: One typical held-out case visually follows the SPH reference, with the largest errors near bottom corners. SPH itself differs from FEM in Appendix B and receives no convergence study.
evaluations.baseline: A time-dependent TLSPH implementation treated as ground truth.

evaluations.metric: Truth-relative L2 interface displacement error by iteration
evaluations.result: R=0.25 is fastest among the plotted cases, while R=5 diverges. The result demonstrates parameter sensitivity, not guaranteed convergence or a selection rule for unseen problems.
evaluations.baseline: N-D at R=0 and several R-D/R-N coefficients.

evaluations.result: ArXiv-v1 Table 3 states about four hours for FEM-SPH versus less than one second for FEM-DeepONet, but omits data generation, training, protocol details, total interface iterations, a disclosed common-work boundary, and a competitive static baseline. Its displayed rate implies roughly 3,600 serial hours for the 900 training cases and 4,000 for all 1,000 cases before neural training.
evaluations.baseline: A time-dependent SPH solver used on a static task.

evaluations.metric: Material methods and interpretation added after canonical arXiv v1
evaluations.result: The later journal author manuscript adds Appendix C amortization formulas and an approximate elastoplastic break-even of 1,124 predictions, plus a caveat that lower neural heat MSE from t=2 to 7 reflects oscillatory FEM error rather than superior generalization. Exact equality including inference is 1,124.052 predictions; these statements are absent from the exact 37-page arXiv v1 audited here.
evaluations.baseline: The canonical arXiv-v1 PDF and source archive pinned by hash in this record.

evaluations.result: ArXiv-v1 static figures list point MSEs and 100,000 or one-million training steps for fully connected tanh networks; essential optimization, normalization, and seed controls are absent. The later author manuscript identifies RTX 2060 neural hardware and two six-core i7-8700 CPUs for FEM data, but not SPH timing hardware or the full training protocol.
evaluations.baseline: No alternative operator architecture, physics-constrained loss, or repeated initialization.

evaluations.setting: Exact arXiv source archive and public artifact routes
evaluations.result: The source contains one TeX manuscript and 23 static raster figures but no code, data, weights, configurations, logs, or figure scripts; no official paper repository was found by the audited exact routes. An unlinked first-author SPH scratch repository is incomplete and contains no DeepONet or full benchmark pipeline.
evaluations.baseline: The information required to reproduce Figures 5-13 and Table 3.

evaluations.result: The audit finds reversed relaxation weights, stale traction indices, incorrect interface definitions, heat value/flux and factor-ten target contradictions, stress/strain output drift, an ambiguous time update, an unreconstructible random field, and multiple material SPH formula and parameter defects. These are execution barriers because no released code identifies the implemented forms.
evaluations.baseline: Agreement among prose, equations, figures, Algorithm 1, and Appendix A.

limitations: No convergence theorem, surrogate-error stability bound, or residual-based reliability guarantee is supplied.
The general coupling prose, Algorithm 1, and specializations disagree on relaxation and interface definitions.
Most evaluation stopping traces use ground-truth error rather than the stated deployable iterate-difference rule.
Only one benchmark trains the learned subdomain from a genuinely different particle model.
All geometries, decompositions, materials, and main physical parameters are fixed within each task.
Independent stress and reciprocal interface networks are not constrained by mechanics or mutual consistency.
The elastoplastic text and Figure C.17 disagree over whether three learned outputs are stresses or strains, and no operator for the reported equivalent plastic strain is specified.
The SPH reference has no particle, kernel, time-step, energy, momentum, or continuum-convergence analysis, and its printed kernel normalization disagrees with the cited implementation.

The pinned arXiv-v1 online speed claim omits the expensive offline dataset and training phases and has no break-even analysis; the later journal author manuscript adds an elastoplastic calculation but not a matched hyperelastic end-to-end protocol.
No hardware, software, tolerance, precision, repeat, or variance protocol supports the wall-time table.
The source release omits code, data, weights, configurations, logs, and figure-generation scripts.
Optimizer, learning rate, batch construction, initialization, normalization, and most splits and seeds are unreported.
Coupled-case statistics, worst-case errors, conservation residuals, and uncertainty calibration are absent.
The Poisson OOD sweep degrades sharply toward rougher inputs and makes the smoother direction look easier.
The heat extrapolation uses a single decaying diffusion family with ambiguous inner-loop indices, contradictory explicit/backward-Euler labels, and targets that can differ by a factor of ten.
Random-field and SPH appendix equations and their essential scale, discretization, and stability parameters are not executable as printed.
No conventional FE-FE, static SPH, ROM, homogenization, or modern hybrid-solver baseline is compared at matched accuracy.
failure_modes: A user implementing page 6 rather than Algorithm 1 can reverse relaxation weights or freeze traction forever.
A learned interface map outside its training support can break contraction and make the Schwarz iteration diverge.
A Robin coefficient selected on one case can be unstable on another; the paper's R=5 case already diverges.
A successive-iterate norm can become small at a false fixed point while the physical residual remains large.
Independent stress-component predictions can violate equilibrium, compatibility, yield, or energy consistency.
Separately learned displacement-to-stress and traction-to-displacement maps can form an inconsistent feedback loop.
FEM-to-network interpolation can alias high-frequency interface functions and dominate the learned error.
The heat inner loop can accidentally advance time more than once if u at n,k is not explicitly frozen.
Long-time dynamics can drift even when one decaying heat trajectory appears stable.
A zero Fourier mode can make the written random-field sampler singular or implementation-dependent.
Confusing spectral decay with correlation length can silently generate a different training distribution from the one claimed.
An incorrect compact-support condition or gradient direction can corrupt the SPH training target.
A factor-ten heat target mismatch or stress-to-strain label switch can produce a numerically plausible model with the wrong units and physical contract.
Training on an unconverged particle solver can faithfully learn discretization artifacts rather than continuum mechanics.
Unreported normalization can fail under new loading amplitudes or material scales.
The offline cost can dominate permanently when the number of online queries is below break-even.
Ground-truth-based stopping and tuning can leak reference information unavailable in deployment.
Fixed interface placement cannot follow fracture, localization, or moving fine-scale phenomena.
reusable_insights: Expose a learned subdomain through a small typed interface: accepted boundary fields, returned conjugate quantities, units, orientation, uncertainty, and residuals.
Test prose, pseudocode, and implementation with one manufactured two-subdomain problem whose update can be calculated by hand.
Validate coupled residual and interface work, not only componentwise surrogate MSE or ground-truth field pictures.
Use truth-independent stopping rules and separately report their calibration against known-solution test cases.
Constrain reciprocal interface operators with cycle consistency or derive both from one energy-consistent model.
Report offline data generation, training, online inference, interface iteration, and break-even query count separately.
Pair every hybrid speed claim with a matched-accuracy conventional solver and the strongest static or reduced-order baseline.
Stress-test distribution shifts in roughness, amplitude, geometry, material parameters, mesh, and subdomain placement independently.
Calibrate uncertainty on interface quantities and fall back to the fine solver when risk or residual exceeds a threshold.
Use manufactured solutions and conservation identities to catch sign, normal-direction, and index errors before training.
Pin random-field zero modes, domain, discretization, normalization, and seeds as part of the dataset specification.
Treat units and conjugate quantity types as machine-checked interface metadata so K-times-derivative and bare-derivative targets cannot be interchanged.
Require particle and mesh convergence before calling either numerical discretization ground truth.
Audit publication-version drift explicitly: preserve the canonical source hash while recording material methods or interpretation added in later revisions.
Separate a promising software architecture from claims of numerical convergence, generality, and amortized benefit.
Treat a learned boundary-condition service as interchangeable so operator architectures can be tested without rewriting the FEM solver.
open_questions: Can one derive a computable bound connecting operator error, interface Jacobian, relaxation, and global coupled-solution error?
Can physical residual or energy descent detect false fixed points without access to a full fine-scale solution?
How should Robin coefficients and relaxation parameters adapt online under surrogate uncertainty?
Can one shared energy-based operator produce both displacement-to-traction and traction-to-displacement responses consistently?
What is the break-even number of queries after accounting for fine-solver data generation, hyperparameter search, training, and maintenance?
Does the method outperform FE-FE Schwarz, static particle solvers, reduced bases, multiscale FEM, and homogenization at matched error?
How does coupled stability change under rougher interface spectra, larger load amplitudes, unseen material laws, and geometry changes?
Can active learning request only the fine-scale simulations that reduce coupled residual or instability risk?
What uncertainty signal is calibrated enough to trigger fine-solver fallback at an interface?
Can a learned subdomain move or grow with a crack tip, plastic zone, shock, or localized error indicator?
Do stochastic microscopic models require distribution-valued operators rather than point-prediction DeepONets?
Which truth-independent stopping rule best predicts actual error across linear, nonlinear, and time-dependent couplings?
Can conformal or variational a posteriori bounds survive the feedback dependence created by an iterative hybrid solver?
How do mesh resolution, interface sensor density, and interpolation order jointly set the attainable accuracy floor?
Which arXiv-v1 conclusions change under the later author's amortization appendix, and does its 1,124-prediction elastoplastic break-even survive matched hardware and end-to-end accounting?
Can automated equation-to-test tooling prevent the relaxation, time-index, and SPH transcription defects seen here?
Would a preregistered multi-seed benchmark reproduce the reported iteration rankings and long-time stability?

competitive_landscape.title: DeepONet: Learning nonlinear operators for identifying differential equations based on the universal approximation theorem of operators
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational architecture used by the paper.
competitive_landscape.difference: DeepONet establishes the branch-trunk operator representation and approximation motivation. The audited paper contributes a numerical-solver interface around that architecture rather than a new operator class.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Operator: Graph Kernel Network for Partial Differential Equations
competitive_landscape.difference: Graph kernel operators explicitly target transfer across discretizations and finite-element representations. They do not supply this paper's concurrent FEM interface loop, but expose the importance of mesh transfer that its fixed-sensor DeepONets do not test.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Domain Decomposition Method: Elliptic Problems
competitive_landscape.difference: DeepDDM exchanges boundary information between neural subdomain solvers and studies overlap-dependent iteration behavior. The audited paper instead retains FEM in one region and uses a pretrained reusable neural operator in the other.

competitive_landscape.title: DeepM&Mnet: Inferring the electroconvection multiphysics fields based on operator approximation by neural networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Predecessor composing multiple pretrained DeepONets for multiphysics.
competitive_landscape.difference: DeepM&Mnet already treats pretrained operators as plug-and-play constraints joining coupled physical fields with sparse measurements. The audited paper replaces the measurement-assimilation composition with an explicit FEM-domain interface iteration.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Mesh-Based Simulation with Graph Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: MeshGraphNets learns adaptive mesh dynamics for several physical systems, including structural mechanics, and reports one-to-two-order online speedups. It replaces the whole rollout rather than embedding a learned local operator in a conventional solver.

competitive_landscape.title: Fourier Neural Operator for Parametric Partial Differential Equations
competitive_landscape.difference: FNO supplies fast global convolutional solution operators and discretization transfer on structured domains. The audited paper selects DeepONet for irregular interface evaluation but never compares architectures within the coupled solver.

competitive_landscape.title: DeepM&Mnet for hypersonics: Predicting the coupled flow and finite-rate chemistry behind a normal shock using neural-network approximation of operators
competitive_landscape.difference: This work composes field-specific DeepONets with sparse measurements and reports in-range and assisted out-of-range behavior. The audited paper instead alternates a standard solver with a local learned boundary map and supplies no sparse correction mechanism.

competitive_landscape.title: Operator learning for predicting multiscale bubble growth dynamics
competitive_landscape.difference: The bubble work learns deterministic macro and stochastic micro regimes with a long-term goal of simplifying heterogeneous handshakes. It predates the paper's FEM-operator iteration and narrows the novelty to the explicit concurrent coupling protocol.

competitive_landscape.title: Error estimates for DeepOnets: A deep learning framework in infinite dimensions
competitive_landscape.relationship: Theory foundation cited for operator approximation.
competitive_landscape.difference: The paper derives approximation and generalization error components for DeepONets. Those standalone operator estimates do not automatically imply contraction or global error bounds after feedback coupling, which the audited work leaves unanalyzed.

competitive_landscape.title: Parallel Physics-Informed Neural Networks via Domain Decomposition
competitive_landscape.relationship: Contemporary neural domain-decomposition and scaling baseline.
competitive_landscape.difference: Parallel cPINNs/XPINNs partition space or time and report weak and strong scaling with heterogeneous subdomain hyperparameters. The audited work uses an offline operator plus FEM but provides no parallel-system or scaling study.

competitive_landscape.title: Finite Basis Physics-Informed Neural Networks (FBPINNs): a scalable domain decomposition approach for solving differential equations
competitive_landscape.difference: FBPINNs use compact overlapping neural bases to address spectral bias and large multiscale domains. They retrain per problem rather than reuse a fine-model operator, but provide a direct alternative to one learned patch inside a decomposition.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Operator: Learning Maps Between Function Spaces
competitive_landscape.relationship: General operator-learning theory and architecture reference.
competitive_landscape.difference: This work formalizes integral neural operators, universal approximation, discretization invariance, and several parameterizations. The audited paper is an application-level coupling design and does not test the claimed discretization invariance of its chosen representation.

competitive_landscape.title: Multiscale modeling of inelastic materials with Thermodynamics-based Artificial Neural Networks (TANN)
competitive_landscape.difference: TANN learns thermodynamically consistent inelastic constitutive state and embeds it in FEM-by-learned homogenization. The audited paper learns local stress components without equivalent thermodynamic constraints but supports explicit interface decomposition.

competitive_landscape.title: An optimization-based strategy for peridynamic-FEM coupling and for the prescription of nonlocal boundary conditions
competitive_landscape.relationship: Contemporary rigorous local-nonlocal mechanics coupling baseline.
competitive_landscape.difference: This method casts 3D peridynamic-FEM interface matching as an optimization problem and studies consistency, accuracy, and numerical convergence. It is not learned, but supplies the kind of coupled-method validation missing from the FEM-DeepONet study.

competitive_landscape.title: Physics-Informed Neural Operator for Learning Partial Differential Equations
competitive_landscape.difference: PINO combines coarse data and higher-resolution PDE constraints to improve fidelity and super-resolution. The audited paper relies on supervised fields and interface derivative penalties without a full residual or mechanics-consistency loss.

competitive_landscape.title: Physics-informed neural networks for learning the homogenized coefficients of multiscale elliptic equations
competitive_landscape.difference: This work learns effective coefficients from multiscale solution data and then solves a homogenized PDE. The audited method retains a spatially localized fine surrogate and explicit interface iteration instead of globally upscaling coefficients.

competitive_landscape.title: The Cost-Accuracy Trade-Off In Operator Learning With Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Evaluation framework for operator cost and accuracy.
competitive_landscape.difference: This study compares parameter, data, evaluation-cost, and accuracy tradeoffs across PCA-Net, DeepONet, PARA-Net, and FNO, including structural mechanics. It highlights why sub-second inference alone is insufficient without offline and accuracy accounting.

competitive_landscape.title: Multifidelity Deep Operator Networks For Data-Driven and Physics-Informed Problems
competitive_landscape.difference: Multifidelity DeepONets combine abundant low-fidelity and scarce high-fidelity data, directly addressing the audited paper's unaccounted fine-solver data cost. They do not provide its online FEM interface loop.

competitive_landscape.title: Generic bounds on the approximation error for physics-informed (and) operator learning
competitive_landscape.difference: This work derives approximation bounds for PINNs, DeepONets, FNOs, and physics-informed operators under PDE stability assumptions. It still does not make the audited hybrid iteration automatically stable, but provides ingredients for a missing end-to-end bound.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards out of distribution generalization for problems in mechanics
competitive_landscape.difference: The study separates covariate, mechanism, and sampling shifts and finds no uniformly robust mechanics OOD method. That taxonomy is substantially stricter than the audited paper's one-parameter random-field smoothness sweep.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning the Stress-Strain Fields in Digital Composites using Fourier Neural Operator
competitive_landscape.difference: FNO predicts full stress and strain fields from varying composite microstructures and tests zero-shot geometry and resolution transfer. It is a global surrogate rather than a coupled local patch, but tackles geometry variation omitted here.

competitive_landscape.title: Fourier Neural Operator with Learned Deformations for PDEs on General Geometries
competitive_landscape.difference: Geo-FNO maps irregular physical domains to a latent regular grid and learns across geometry families. It directly weakens the paper's then-current FNO geometry objection and addresses a major fixed-geometry limitation.

competitive_landscape.title: Multiscale Neural Operator: Learning Fast and Grid-independent PDE Solvers
competitive_landscape.difference: This hybrid surrogate keeps known large-scale dynamics and learns only the unresolved closure with a grid-independent operator. It offers a closure-based alternative to spatially replacing a local fine solver.

competitive_landscape.title: Blending Neural Operators and Relaxation Methods in PDE Numerical Solvers
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest same-group hybrid iterative solver successor.
competitive_landscape.difference: HINTS alternates DeepONet and classical relaxation to balance spectral error modes and studies transferable iterative acceleration. It integrates at the correction/preconditioning level rather than assigning a learned spatial subdomain.

competitive_landscape.title: GNOT: A General Neural Operator Transformer for Operator Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: Flexible irregular-mesh and multiscale operator successor.
competitive_landscape.difference: GNOT handles multiple input functions and irregular meshes with heterogeneous attention and geometric gating interpreted as soft domain decomposition. It offers an architectural alternative to multiple independently trained fixed-grid DeepONets.

competitive_landscape.title: Efficient Error Certification for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: The work certifies worst-case PDE residuals over continuous domains instead of relying on finite-point comparisons. Its guarantees target PINNs rather than operator-feedback loops, but illustrate a stronger validation standard than field plots and mean MSE.

competitive_landscape.title: Geometry-Informed Neural Operator for Large-Scale 3D PDEs
competitive_landscape.difference: GINO combines point-cloud geometry encoding with latent-grid operator layers for large 3D PDEs. It addresses complex geometry and scale more directly than the audited fixed 2D patches, while not retaining an external FEM domain.

competitive_landscape.title: A hybrid physics-informed neural network based multiscale solver as a partial differential equation constrained optimization problem
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct FEM-neural multiscale successor with variational analysis.
competitive_landscape.difference: This method couples a fine-scale PINN objective to a coarse finite-element PDE constraint and analyzes the resulting function space and algorithm. It integrates coarse physics during training rather than alternating a frozen DeepONet subdomain online.

competitive_landscape.title: Multifidelity domain decomposition-based physics-informed neural networks and operators for time-dependent problems
competitive_landscape.difference: The work combines multifidelity stacking with temporal FBPINN decomposition and extends the design to physics-informed DeepONets. It targets multiscale time training rather than the audited paper's ambiguous nested online heat update.

competitive_landscape.title: Conformalized-DeepONet: A Distribution-Free Framework for Uncertainty Quantification in Deep Operator Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Conformalized DeepONet adds finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees to probabilistic, Bayesian, and quantile variants. Such intervals could support interface fallback, which the audited deterministic coupling lacks.

competitive_landscape.title: Uncertainty quantification for deeponets with ensemble kalman inversion
competitive_landscape.difference: Ensemble Kalman inversion trains DeepONet ensembles and estimates predictive uncertainty under limited noisy data. The audited work explicitly defers noisy microscopic data and reports no epistemic uncertainty.

competitive_landscape.title: Bridging scales in multiscale bubble growth dynamics with correlated fluctuations using neural operator learning
competitive_landscape.difference: The composite model joins a mean DeepONet with an LSTM for correlated microscopic fluctuations across DPD and continuum regimes. It begins to address stochastic fine dynamics that the audited deterministic SPH example lists only as future work.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Preconditioning Operator for Efficient PDE Solves
competitive_landscape.difference: NPO trains operator preconditioners with condition and residual losses and evaluates Krylov convergence on uniform and irregular meshes. It preserves the classical solver's correction path rather than replacing a local physics model.

competitive_landscape.title: Time Marching Neural Operator FE Coupling: AI Accelerated Physics Modeling
competitive_landscape.difference: This work extends overlapping Schwarz FE-DeepONet coupling with embedded time stepping and adaptive learned-subdomain evolution across static, quasi-static, and dynamic solid mechanics. It directly targets error accumulation and moving fine regions left open in 2022.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural-operator element method: Efficient and scalable finite element method enabled by reusable neural operators
competitive_landscape.difference: NOEM inserts reusable neural-operator elements into the FEM variational assembly, avoiding dense subdomain meshes while retaining weak-form coupling. It offers a more mechanically integrated alternative to iterative boundary exchange and evaluates broader geometry and discontinuous-coefficient cases.

competitive_landscape.title: A Learning-based Domain Decomposition Method
competitive_landscape.difference: L-DDM reuses one neural operator trained on simple domains across complicated decomposed geometries and provides an abstract approximation-existence result. It targets geometry and microstructure transfer absent from the fixed-domain FEM-DeepONet examples.

competitive_landscape.title: Physics-Informed DeepONet Coupled with FEM for Convective Transport in Porous Media with Sharp Gaussian Sources
competitive_landscape.difference: This framework solves Darcy flow with FEM and passes velocity into a physics-informed DeepONet for transport, adding adaptive trunk sampling and an official implementation. It is sequential multiphysics composition rather than iterative spatial Schwarz coupling.

competitive_landscape.title: Variationally correct operator learning: Reduced basis neural operator with a posteriori error estimation
competitive_landscape.difference: RBNO uses conforming reduced bases and FOSLS losses equivalent to PDE error norms, with a computable a posteriori estimator and error decomposition including discretization and statistical terms. That is a stronger reliability contract than pointwise MSE for the audited learned patch.

competitive_landscape.title: Test-time Generalization for Physics through Neural Operator Splitting
competitive_landscape.difference: Neural operator splitting searches compositions of pretrained dynamics at test time for unseen parameters and physics. It addresses novel-physics extrapolation rather than trusting one frozen local operator outside its training family.

competitive_landscape.title: Are Deep Learning Based Hybrid PDE Solvers Reliable? Why Training Paradigms and Update Strategies Matter
competitive_landscape.difference: This study shows HINTS and Fourier-neural hybrids can stagnate at false fixed points with large physical residuals and proposes physics-aware Anderson acceleration. It directly validates the concern that small iterate updates need not mean the audited coupling is correct.

competitive_landscape.title: Frequency Bias and OOD Generalization in Neural Operators under a Variable-Coefficient Wave Equation
competitive_landscape.difference: This work independently varies input frequency and coefficient smoothness and finds sharp high-frequency degradation, especially for FNO. Its design reinforces the need to separate the roughness directions obscured in the audited alpha sweep.

competitive_landscape.title: A Non-Overlapping Schwarz Hybrid Finite Element-Neural Operator Framework for Solid Mechanics on Irregular Domains
competitive_landscape.difference: This method replaces overlap with Neumann-Dirichlet exchange, uses Point-DeepONet on irregular point clouds, and derives strain and stress from displacement to enforce kinematic consistency. Those choices directly repair geometry and independent-stress weaknesses in the 2022 design.

competitive_landscape.title: Conformal Prediction for Neural Operators: Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification in Physics Simulation
competitive_landscape.difference: This work adds split-conformal prediction intervals and adaptive widths to FNO heat simulation. Marginal coverage alone does not certify feedback stability, but it provides a deployment signal entirely absent from the audited deterministic interface.

competitive_landscape.title: Multipole Graph Neural Operator for Parametric Partial Differential Equations
competitive_landscape.difference: MGNO combines local and long-range graph-kernel interactions with linear-complexity motivation. Its multiscale structure is architectural rather than an explicit heterogeneous FEM-neural subdomain coupling.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning the solution operator of parametric partial differential equations with physics-informed DeepOnets
competitive_landscape.difference: This method trains solution operators with PDE residuals and can reduce dependence on paired solver data. The audited paper uses supervised fine-solver targets and does not enforce the coupled system's full physics during training.

competitive_landscape.title: Mosaic Flows: A Transferable Deep Learning Framework for Solving PDEs on Unseen Domains
competitive_landscape.difference: Mosaic Flows trains a local square-domain solver once and iteratively tiles it across larger unseen domains and boundary conditions. It already combines reuse with stitching; the audited paper remains distinct through heterogeneous FEM-DeepONet mechanics coupling.

competitive_landscape.title: A physics-informed variational DeepONet for predicting the crack path in brittle materials
competitive_landscape.difference: The variational DeepONet mixes data and energy physics for fracture-path prediction and examines extrapolation. It is a standalone global operator, but uses a stronger mechanics constraint than the audited componentwise stress networks.

competitive_landscape.title: When Do Extended Physics-Informed Neural Networks (XPINNs) Improve Generalization?
competitive_landscape.difference: The work shows decomposition can simplify local target functions but reduce data per region and sometimes hurt generalization. It cautions against assuming a learned patch generalizes merely because the global domain was divided.

competitive_landscape.title: A comprehensive and fair comparison of two neural operators (with practical extensions) based on FAIR data
competitive_landscape.relationship: Paper-time DeepONet versus FNO evaluation baseline.
competitive_landscape.difference: This comparison studies accuracy, speed, noise, and geometry extensions for DeepONet and FNO. The audited paper cites it to justify DeepONet but does not repeat a coupled-solver architecture comparison.

competitive_landscape.title: An equivariant neural operator for developing nonlocal tensorial constitutive models
competitive_landscape.difference: This operator hard-codes translation and permutation invariance plus rotational equivariance for tensor constitutive closure. It demonstrates how physical tensor structure can be enforced instead of hoping separate generic networks preserve it.

competitive_landscape.title: Nonlocal Kernel Network (NKN): a Stable and Resolution-Independent Deep Neural Network
competitive_landscape.difference: NKN explicitly motivates stability and resolution independence for nonlocal operators. The audited paper instead reports empirical coupled convergence without an operator or feedback-stability guarantee.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep transfer operator learning for partial differential equations under conditional shift
competitive_landscape.difference: This method detects and adapts operator models to geometry or dynamics shifts using target data. The audited coupling instead assumes its offline interface distribution covers online states and offers no shift detector.

competitive_landscape.title: Fourier Neural Solver for large sparse linear algebraic systems
competitive_landscape.difference: FNS alternates FFT-based neural corrections with stationary iteration and analyzes frequency behavior. It preserves a full-system residual-correction path rather than replacing one physical subdomain.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Geometry Transferability of the Hybrid Iterative Numerical Solver for Differential Equations
competitive_landscape.difference: The paper explicitly studies whether HINTS transfers between geometries. The audited learned microregion remains geometrically fixed and never isolates geometry transfer.

competitive_landscape.title: Augmented Physics-Informed Neural Networks (APINNs): A gating network-based soft domain decomposition methodology
competitive_landscape.difference: APINNs learn soft partitions and parameter sharing and show that decomposition choice can strongly affect performance. The audited paper fixes every region and interface manually.

competitive_landscape.title: Comparison of Neural FEM and Neural Operator Methods for applications in Solid Mechanics
competitive_landscape.difference: This study contrasts neural FEM and neural operators, emphasizing that operator amortization requires costly training and can trade accuracy for repeated-query speed. It provides missing calibration for the audited online-only timing claim.

competitive_landscape.title: Breaking Boundaries: Distributed Domain Decomposition with Scalable Physics-Informed Neural PDE Solvers
competitive_landscape.difference: This work distributes Mosaic Flow training and inference and reports domains up to 4,096 times the training size on 32 GPUs. It offers system-scale evidence absent from the audited fixed examples, though not FEM mechanics coupling.

competitive_landscape.title: DeepOnet Based Preconditioning Strategies For Solving Parametric Linear Systems of Equations
competitive_landscape.difference: The method uses DeepONet inverse actions or trunk bases as preconditioners while Krylov iteration enforces the global system. It is more tightly residual-corrected than trusting a learned local subdomain response.

competitive_landscape.title: Material-Response-Informed DeepONet and its Application to Polycrystal Stress-strain Prediction in Crystal Plasticity
competitive_landscape.difference: Material-response inputs and few-shot transfer support changes in materials and loading. The audited stress networks are tied to one geometry, constitutive setting, and narrow excitation family.

competitive_landscape.title: Enhancing Multiscale Simulations with Constitutive Relations-Aware Deep Operator Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: This approach embeds microscale constitutive relations and homogenization in DeepONet for quasi-static solids, addressing data efficiency and mechanical consistency. It uses FE-squared-style homogenization rather than spatial interface coupling.

competitive_landscape.title: MgFNO: Multi-grid Architecture Fourier Neural Operator for Parametric Partial Differential Equations
competitive_landscape.difference: MgFNO introduces multigrid training and architecture for cross-resolution efficiency. It addresses scale transfer inside the operator, not the audited paper's heterogeneous solver boundary.

competitive_landscape.title: Separable DeepONet: Breaking the Curse of Dimensionality in Physics-Informed Machine Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Coordinate factorization and forward-mode differentiation make collocation scaling linear in dimension-specific resolution. This targets training scalability, which the audited million-step networks do not quantify.

competitive_landscape.title: Operator Learning with Domain Decomposition for Geometry Generalization in PDE Solving
competitive_landscape.difference: Schwarz Neural Inference composes local neural operators on arbitrary geometries and gives convergence-rate and error-bound analysis. It is all-neural rather than FEM-neural, but directly addresses theory and geometry gaps in the 2022 loop.

competitive_landscape.title: Hybrid deep learning and iterative methods for accelerated solutions of viscous incompressible flow
competitive_landscape.difference: HyDEA combines DeepONet search directions with CG or PCG refinement and tests transfer across geometry, Reynolds number, and resolution. It retains classical convergence correction instead of making a frozen learned patch authoritative.

competitive_landscape.title: A Neural Operator based Hybrid Microscale Model for Multiscale Simulation of Rate-Dependent Materials
competitive_landscape.difference: The hybrid microscale model retains constitutive relations and internal variables inside an FE-squared-style viscoelastic operator. It tests rate-dependent structure absent from the static hyperelastic SPH surrogate.

competitive_landscape.title: DD-DeepONet: Domain decomposition and DeepONet for solving partial differential equations in three application scenarios
competitive_landscape.difference: DD-DeepONet decomposes rectangle and cuboid domains and uses stretching across geometry, boundary, and parameter variations while reducing memory. It remains all-neural but exercises broader reuse scenarios.

competitive_landscape.title: MD-PNOP: Equation-Recast Neural Operators for Minimal-Data Extrapolation and PDE Solver Acceleration
competitive_landscape.difference: MD-PNOP recasts parameter changes as source terms and uses neural predictions to initialize iterative PDE solves, so the full physics remains enforced. This is safer under extrapolation than a surrogate-only region.

competitive_landscape.title: Hybrid Iterative Solvers with Geometry-Aware Neural Preconditioners for Parametric PDEs
competitive_landscape.difference: Geo-DeepONet consumes finite-element geometry and works with relaxation or Krylov solvers on arbitrary unstructured meshes. It provides geometry and discretization transfer beyond the audited fixed interface sensors.

competitive_landscape.title: ANCHOR: Error-Controlled Adaptive Numerical Correction for Neural Operator Time Marching
competitive_landscape.difference: ANCHOR monitors a residual moving average and triggers high-fidelity corrections without ground truth across long extrapolative rollouts. It supplies the deployable correction signal missing from the audited heat and interface stopping rules.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural-Schwarz Tiling for Geometry-Universal PDE Solving at Scale
competitive_landscape.difference: NEST assembles learned local voxel solvers over unseen large 3D neo-Hookean solids with overlapping Schwarz and partition of unity. It provides far stronger shape, size, boundary, and nonlinear-mechanics scaling evidence than the fixed 2D examples.

competitive_landscape.title: Machine learning materials physics: Deep neural networks trained on elastic free energy data from martensitic microstructures predict homogenized stress fields with high accuracy
competitive_landscape.difference: This method learns elastic free energy and obtains homogenized stresses by differentiation, preserving hyperelastic structure. It is an older alternative to directly regressing separate stress fields without a shared potential.

competitive_landscape.title: Machine-learning of nonlocal kernels for anomalous subsurface transport from breakthrough curves
competitive_landscape.difference: The work identifies a nonlocal kernel from observations instead of replacing a spatial solver region with a black-box field map. It represents an interpretable model-discovery alternative cited by the target.

competitive_landscape.title: Approximate Bayesian Neural Operators: Uncertainty Quantification for Parametric PDEs
competitive_landscape.difference: Approximate Bayesian operators expose posterior uncertainty that can flag poor predictions. The audited coupling returns deterministic point fields and has no uncertainty-aware fallback or relaxation rule.

competitive_landscape.title: PDEBENCH: An Extensive Benchmark for Scientific Machine Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: PDEBench compares models across PDEs, resolutions, conservation metrics, and rollouts. Its breadth and metric discipline exceed the target's four custom cases and pointwise error pictures.

competitive_landscape.title: Reliable extrapolation of deep neural operators informed by physics or sparse observations
competitive_landscape.difference: This work quantifies function-space shift and finds data-only operators generally interpolation-limited unless physics or sparse observations correct them. It directly narrows the target's broad generalization reading of one alpha and time sweep.

competitive_landscape.title: A Neural Network Transformer Model for Composite Microstructure Homogenization
competitive_landscape.difference: The model conditions on composite microstructure and predicts history-dependent homogenized response across arbitrary composites. It is a homogenization alternative to retaining an explicit fine spatial subdomain.

competitive_landscape.title: Probabilistic neural operators for functional uncertainty quantification
competitive_landscape.difference: Probabilistic neural operators learn output-function distributions with proper scoring rules and evaluate long-trajectory calibration. The audited model supplies only point estimates and mean-square errors.

competitive_landscape.title: On-the-fly construction of surrogate constitutive models for concurrent multiscale mechanical analysis through probabilistic machine learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Gaussian-process surrogates replace FE-squared micromodel solves online and use uncertainty-triggered anchor evaluations, avoiding the target's large fixed offline corpus while supplying an adaptive fine-solver fallback signal.

competitive_landscape.title: A neural network multigrid solver for the Navier-Stokes equations
competitive_landscape.difference: Classical coarse multigrid is augmented by recurrent-network fine corrections on reusable local patches; unlike the target, it is not a neural operator or a two-subdomain Schwarz interface coupling.

competitive_landscape.title: MIONet: Learning multiple-input operators via tensor product
competitive_landscape.difference: MIONet jointly represents several input functions, offering a principled route for interface state, geometry, material parameters, and history that the target handles through fixed single-function component maps.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Deep Implicit Fourier Neural Operators (IFNOs) with Applications to Heterogeneous Material Modeling
competitive_landscape.difference: A monolithic implicit operator models heterogeneous, defective, hyperelastic, anisotropic, and brittle materials rather than spatially isolating a fine region and iterating an interface.

competitive_landscape.title: A Physics-Guided Neural Operator Learning Approach to Model Biological Tissues from Digital Image Correlation Measurements
competitive_landscape.difference: It documents data-only operator degradation under out-of-distribution loading and improvement from partial physics, directly challenging the target's unmonitored interface-input generalization assumption.

competitive_landscape.title: Multifidelity deep neural operators for efficient learning of partial differential equations with application to fast inverse design of nanoscale heat transport
competitive_landscape.difference: Residual coupling of low- and high-fidelity DeepONets reduces expensive fine data, directly addressing the target's excluded high-fidelity data-generation burden.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Interface Conditions in Domain Decomposition Solvers
competitive_landscape.difference: A graph-convolutional network and unsupervised loss learn optimized interface modifications that transfer from small training problems to large unstructured systems; it learns the coupling operator rather than replacing fine-domain physics.

competitive_landscape.title: Integrated Finite Element Neural Network (I-FENN) for non-local continuum damage mechanics
competitive_landscape.difference: The physics-informed network is embedded in element residual and Jacobian construction, making tangent information explicit instead of using the target's black-box alternating boundary exchange.
